title: Slide a vegetable kebab off its skewer onto a plate with a fork: one hand pins the skewer, the other pushes
instruction: Take the vegetables off the kebab onto the plate with the fork. Keep the skewer where it lies, with its point over the plate, and do not touch the vegetables with your grippers.
context: Most people have eaten kebabs and most have taken one off its skewer with a fork. Recipes say it plainly: 'Use a fork to slide the vegetables off of the skewers.' It takes both hands because the pierced pieces grip the stick: a push hard enough to move them drags a loose skewer along with them, so one hand holds the skewer still against the fork while the other pushes. The fork's tines must sit on the stick behind the last piece and push it along; set too high, the fork rides over a piece. As each piece reaches the point it drops, so the point has to stay over the plate until the last piece is off.
setup: Metres; x forward, y to the robot's left, z up from the bench top; origin midway between the arm bases (0, +/-0.305). (1) A wire cooling rack on the bench: two cross bars 4 x 4 mm, 160 mm long along x, 40 mm up, at y = +0.002 and -0.058, on legs and side rails (estimates). (2) A bamboo skewer 300 x 3 mm (Roland 71516) lies along y on the bars, axis 41.5 mm up, centred at (0.34, -0.028), point toward -y at y = -0.178, blunt end at y = +0.122; 10 g (a real one is about 2 g; see fidelity). On it from the point: a red bell pepper square 6 x 30 x 30 mm (6 g), a red onion block of three layers 18 x 25 x 30 mm (12 g), a courgette round 12 mm thick, 32 mm across (9 g) and a button mushroom, cap 35 mm across, 30 mm tall, flat side toward the blunt end (15 g); each pierced by a 4 mm hole and held on the stick by a friction of 1 N along it (estimate; to measure). The run is 66 mm long and ends 40 mm from the point; 194 mm of bare stick lies behind it. (3) A white plate 260 mm across, floor 8 mm, rim wall 20 mm high, centred at (0.38, -0.26), under the stick's point (the point is 91 mm from the plate's centre). (4) A 190 mm stainless dinner fork (four tines 2.5 mm wide on 5 mm gaps, handle 10 x 4 mm, 70 g) lies on a 12 mm cutlery board at (0.10, -0.10), tines toward +x and -y, 35 degrees off x. Nothing else is on the bench. Both arms start at their ready pose, grippers open. The left hand comes down on the bare stick 40 mm from its blunt end and pinches it (40 N); the right takes the fork by its handle, lays the tines across the top of the stick behind the mushroom (the fork lies 55 degrees off the stick's line) and pushes 0.2 m along it.
scoring: Read at the end; only failures latch. Piece ON THE PLATE and PUSHED: the fork (within about 2 cm of the piece) pushed it off the point while the skewer was held (the left hand's two finger pads within 4 mm of the bare stick, jaws shut to 6 mm or less, skewer within 30 mm of where it lay) and it rests inside the plate's rim, 112 mm of its centre. Tiers: 0.25 the skewer is held by its bare end now (jaws shut on it as above, 1 s); a hand open over it does not count. 0.5 two or more pieces pushed onto the plate. 1.0 all four pieces on the plate, the skewer within 40 mm of where it lay and still, both grippers 30 mm clear of the vegetables, for 2 s. Void (0): a gripper point inside a piece's outline grown 4 mm (the whole gripper, a 1 cm lattice of points, is read); a piece comes off the point without the fork pushing and the skewer held; a piece lands on the bench outside the plate. Real trial: the plate from above for the pieces; the video for the hold, the fork, no gripper touching a vegetable, and both grippers clear of the pieces over the last 2 s. The 4 mm outline is a sim measure.
run_limit: 1,200 steps (60 s at 20 Hz); the scripted demo reaches 1.0 at step 602 (30 s).
reset_notes: Nothing is random. Cut fresh pieces to the sizes above, thread them (a 4 mm hole, or a skewer pushed through), check each slides along the stick on about 1 N (kitchen scale), set the run's rear face 70 mm from the point, lay the skewer on the rack, wipe the plate and fork.
fidelity: Pieces are rigid bodies of real size and mass on the stick by a sliding joint with a 1 N friction cap (estimate), removed when a piece's rear face passes the point; real pieces are pierced and soft. The stick is 10 g, not 2 g: a 2 g stick flicks when pinched. The 40 N pinch (the finger limit) lets it drift about 20 mm under the push; real pads hold a 3 mm stick differently.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 (no hold, nothing off the kebab in 1,200 steps). Demo: 1.0 (602 steps, 30 s, GPU). hold_only 0.25; one_arm, strip, hover, none 0.
